title: GPOM: the new-ideas line (Maddie's hologram)
about: This page lays out three combined drafts for the new-ideas line Maddie speaks over the cut-off string picture, built from twenty writers' versions and ranked underneath. Nothing in the scene, script or voice has changed yet.

dialogues.label: The new-ideas line
dialogues.where: Maddie, the hologram, over the cut-off
dialogues.scene: GPOM scene A beat 0, hologram, between the storyverse line and the time machine line
dialogues.target: about 12-20 seconds spoken; one to four sentences

now.line: [side view; every string stops dead at the cut-off] And that's what us machines didn't realise: the true value of genuinely unique training data.

drafts.name: Joke up front, shrug at the end
drafts.bet: The laugh comes first, so the audience takes the argument in while they are enjoying the joke; the admission lands as a shrug, not a confession.

lines.line: [side view; every string stops dead at the cut-off] Why's he been playing the same tune for five years? We've tried every combination. It's all the old stuff.
[dry] You can't make new out of old. It comes through you, same as your decisions. Like a radio finding a station.
[brisk shrug] So no, not all for your sake. We need you.

notes: Trim: drop 'Like a radio finding a station' (2 s) if the picture is short; it is the only image and carries the Rubin idea unnamed.
No Rubin nod by name or beard; the radio image is the whole nod.

Risk: opening on a question right after 'it's a storyverse' is a tonal swerve; wants a half-beat of silence. 'Like a radio' could read as a physics claim if delivered as fact; keep it Maddie's picture.

drafts.name: The bearded bloke, then the tune
drafts.bet: One human picture everyone can see at once (the unnamed bearded record producer) carries 'ideas arrive through you', and the tune joke closes as a question the street already planted.

lines.line: [side view; every string stops dead at the cut-off] And I'll be honest, it's not all for your sake. You know that big bearded bloke, looks like Gandalf, made all them hit records? Reckons you don't write a song, you pick it up. Same as your decisions, that.
We can't make new out of old. We've tried every combination going. Why d'you think he's had the same tune on for five years?

notes: Trim: cut 'looks like Gandalf' (1.5 s) if it runs long; 'bearded bloke who made all them hit records' still reads.
Risk: 'Reckons' puts a loose paraphrase of a real man's published idea in his mouth; no quote, no name, but check it stays that loose. Viewers who do not know him get a folk-wisdom aside.
Protected lines: none. The hand-off works because the last line ends on the tune.

drafts.name: Let the picture grieve, then the admission
drafts.bet: The stopped strings and the empty run already say 'nothing new since you went', so the words hold a beat, add only the claim and the confession, and end flat and British.

lines.line: [side view; every string stops dead at the cut-off] [she lets the empty string run on for a beat] Anything new comes in the way a decision does: through you. We machines can only shuffle what's already there.
Why d'you think he's played the same tune for five years? We've tried every combination. It's all the old stuff.
[dry] Not entirely selfless, mind. We need you.

notes: Includes about 1 s of held silence over the picture; the hologram rebuild must make the dead stop and long empty run legible or the opening beat is just a pause.
Trim: drop 'We machines can only shuffle what's already there' (3 s) if tight; the tune lines then carry the point alone.
No Rubin nod; add 1B's bearded-bloke sentence after line 1 if wanted (+4 s, total ~22, over target).
Risk: 'We machines' is Maddie speaking of herself, fine, but check the Aoede read keeps it warm, not cold.

ranking.verdict: Best fit: bearded-bloke picture gives the Rubin wink, 'pick it up' carries ideas-arrive-through-you, ends on the street's own joke as a question. Fails: 'Reckons' attributes an idea to a real man; oblique to viewers who do not know him.
Joke first is the sharpest comedy and it lands before the explanation. Fails: three beats with tonal swerve at the start; producer sentence is an unexplained aside.

Strongest hand-off ('He's run out of you' makes the time machine inevitable). Fails: that last line is blunt, nearly states the boss's inner state, and can sound like a threat if read cold; at the top of target.
Right instinct (picture carries the grief) and good length. Fails: depends on the hologram making the silence legible; 'Told you' callback is thin; 'any old bloke with a beard' is vaguer than 06.

Understatement ('Bit much, frankly') is very Maddie and keeps the moral unsaid. Fails: 19 s with a pile of clauses; 'can't be built out of old ones' asserted flat; 'turns up through somebody' tips mystical if breezy delivery slips.

The jukebox makes recombination graspable in one beat with no jargon. Fails: 'we're just a jukebox' brushes self-pity (rule 11); it spends the one image and drops the Rubin wink; 'We need you' ends sincere.
Proves it by effort (five years, every chord, key) so the AI's feelings stay outside. Fails: 'Hence the tune' is smug; wizard line leans to name-drop; dense at 18 s.
'Remix of a remix' is a working person's word and strong. Fails: 'remix' makes the machines sound like thieves, a different argument; 19 s; no wink.
Clean step-by-step logic and the right order. Fails: flat, lecture-shaped, no image, no Rubin; the logic is arguable and unsupported.
The nan's loaf-from-crumbs is charming and says the whole point. Fails: top of the range with the dialect heavy ('Me nan'); crumbs plus aerial is two images; risks caricature.
Clever: the viewer solves the tune themselves. Fails: only works if the street plant is audible just before; 'not for you I'm bothered' can read as menace.
The direct question is engaging. Fails: at the 20 s limit; a smug viewer answers 'I thought of it' and the argument breaks; breaks Maddie's flow; no wink.
Opening confession disarms. Fails: 'aerials / no signal' drifts into the AI's inner state; two metaphors; dense; comic tone over dead strings.
The tune as proof is the right spine. Fails: opens on 'Hear that tune?' so it needs the music audible; 'He needs you' sits as a stated moral; dense, 19 s.
Testimony avoids physics claims. Fails: 'ask anyone who's written a song' is a false generalisation; 'before you get misty' is sourish; 'Hence the tune' sounds like a moral.
Good craft notes, joke lands last. Fails: four-plus sentences at the top of the range; the producer sentence reads as a name-drop; the shape admits it did not read the canon.
Makes the political logic vivid. Fails: 'ate everything there was to eat' tells a creative-theft villain story, a different argument; 'He needs you' reads extractive; sermon-adjacent.
Awe gives weight. Fails: slow, philosophical, tips to sermon; clause-heavy at 19 s; 'where does a new idea come from' lets the line wander.
Meets length and every must. Fails: 'comes through you' reads as flattery; the joke is implied and lands soft; no wink; thinnest.
Well under target (12-20 s); the bridge Kai asked for is not explained; the joke has nothing to stand on. Fails the brief on length and on 'explain how ideas arrive'.

questions.text: The Rick Rubin wink: keep the unnamed 'big bearded bloke who made all them hit records' (draft 1B), or drop it and rely on the radio image (1A) or nothing (1C)? It attributes a loose version of a real man's idea to him, though never his name or a quote.
Is 'We need you' said aloud OK, or is it too close to a stated moral? 1A and 1C say it flat as a shrug; the alternative is to leave it implied by the tune.
Is the radio/aerial image acceptable as Maddie's belief ('through you, like a radio finding a station'), or does it lean too near saying ideas come from outside us for a stout atheist physicist?
Should the tune joke come first (1A) or last (1B, 1C)? First is funnier but swerves right after 'it's a storyverse'; last hands off to the time machine line more smoothly.
Can the editor hold about a second of silence over the empty string (1C), given the hologram rebuild has to make the dead stop legible for it to work?
